j.learned_fact: Rabbits eat grass and leaves, not cake, and chewing keeps their ever-growing teeth worn down; also that books start at the front and the marks are words. Slight exaggeration: one leaf would not visibly shorten a rabbit's teeth.
j.thinking_skill: applies information from a picture to solve a real problem (notices cause and effect)
j.notes: The "teeth looked a tiny bit shorter" after a single leaf is a false shortcut; the story also juggles two lessons (print concepts and rabbit diet) which slightly splits focus for a four-year-old.

j.learned_fact: A tummy growls when it is empty and goes quiet after you eat; also hot pot vs. cold cup.
j.thinking_skill: notices one cause and effect (empty tummy → growl)
j.notes: Charming and age-appropriate, but the "rolled up her sleeve" detail is odd/non-sequitur and the hot/cold moment feels inserted rather than part of the plot.

j.learned_fact: Sound is vibration: when the drum shakes, the air carries the "wiggles" and your eardrum shakes, which is how you hear. (Accurate, though feeling your outer ear shake from a small tap is a stretch.)
j.thinking_skill: notices one cause and effect (drum taps → ear shakes, stops when tapping stops)
j.notes: The drum solves nothing about the hot soup, so the plot is two bolted-together bits; the second paragraph is a checklist of five senses plus counting, and Daddy delivers the science as a mini-lecture.

j.learned_fact: Yeast is a tiny living thing that eats sugar in dough and makes bubbles that make it rise; also red + yellow = orange.
j.thinking_skill: notices a cause and effect (bubbles make the dough big)
j.notes: Two lessons (colour mixing and yeast) are crammed together, with the yeast explanation delivered as a flat adult definition; the "orange, just like the bread" link is odd and the gallery/kitchen setting is implausible. For a 3-year-old, vocabulary is mostly fine but the yeast science and the pace are above the band.

j.learned_fact: Sweat comes out of tiny holes (pores) in the skin and cools you as it dries — true, though the story's trigger (warm tap water on hands) is an implausible cause of sweating.
j.thinking_skill: restates a cause and effect pair told to him
j.notes: Mama's pore/evaporation explanation is a bolted-on mini-lecture, and the premise that warm handwashing makes a child sweat down his face is physiologically odd. Thomas's "good thinking" line is parroted, not reasoned.

j.learned_fact: Flushing sends water from the tank into the bowl, and the rushing water pulls things down the pipe — accurate.
j.thinking_skill: notices one cause and effect (water pulls the tissue down)
j.notes: Three loosely linked episodes (coat, toilet, sheep) with no unifying arc; the toilet paragraph reads as an inserted science moment and the sheep ending is arbitrary.

j.learned_fact: A fridge is cold inside but warm at the back, because it moves heat out of the box — accurate.
j.thinking_skill: compares front and back by touch and infers a cause
j.notes: Sentences are short enough for age 4, but the heat-transfer inference ("the fridge pushes the warm out") is beyond a 4-year-old's reasoning and sounds like an adult speaking through Miles; the two episodes (tablet, fridge) feel stitched together, and details like the bus and coat hook are unused.

j.learned_fact: A letter needs an address written on it, or the post office will return it to the sender. (But the story implies a drawn stamp is acceptable, which is false — real postage is required.)
j.thinking_skill: infers the cause of the failure and fixes it ("It needs Grandma's street")
j.notes: The mail carrier's explanation is a small lecture, and the drawn stamp muddles the lesson. For a 3-year-old the plot has too many steps (sorting building, three-day delay, turn-taking subplot) and phrases like "empty of words" are abstract.

j.learned_fact: "The scab is a lid. New skin grows under it." — accurate: a scab protects the wound while new skin forms. (But "put it back" is bad advice; a detached scab cannot be replaced.)
j.thinking_skill: applies a remembered fact to explain what a scab is for
j.notes: Sentences are short enough for a 3-year-old, but the blood/picked-scab topic and words like "store of bandages" and "librarian" are off for JK; the health fact is dropped in as a mini-definition and the advice to "put it back" is wrong. The bandage-store line is an odd non-sequitur.

j.learned_fact: Fog is a cloud that has come down low to the ground; it feels cool and damp.
j.thinking_skill: applies a category (cloud) to a new instance (fog) he can reach
j.notes: Some lines feel inserted to drill time words ("Yesterday/Today/Tomorrow", "Now/Later") and the odd "The wet would stick to his shoes too" is awkward for a 3-year-old; "That was his problem" is narratorly rather than child-like.

j.learned_fact: Cold butter is hard and tears bread; warmth softens it so it spreads smoothly. Also 3 + 3 = 6 when six cookies are shared equally.
j.thinking_skill: identifies a cause (cold butter) and tests a fix, then shares by one-to-one counting
j.notes: Two separate lessons (butter physics, fair sharing) stacked in one short piece feels curriculum-driven; sentence count and some phrasing ("Soft butter spreads easy," "Same same!") sit a little above/awkward for a four-year-old listener.

j.learned_fact: Things in a store are not free; you give money to the shopkeeper to get them, and she uses the money to buy more stock and pay workers.
j.thinking_skill: generalizes a rule from one observed exchange ("you give money, you get things")
j.notes: Grandpa's explanation about restocking and paying employees is an adult economics lecture beyond a three-year-old, and Madeline's tidy summarizing lines sound like an author's thesis rather than a toddler. Sentences are suitably short, but the concept load and dialogue voice skew older.

j.learned_fact: Sweat dries on the skin and cools the body down (accurate, though evaporation isn't named).
j.thinking_skill: notices one cause and effect (sweat drying → feeling cooler)
j.notes: The science line "Sweat dries and cools me down" is stated twice as a recited formula rather than discovered, and the grill-safety bit is bolted on with no connection to the plot. Sentences are short enough for a 3-year-old listener, but the self-explaining child and the abstract concept fit an older reader.

j.learned_fact: Sharing one-for-you-one-for-me splits six cookies into three each; but the story first says ten cookies, so the arithmetic is inconsistent/false.
j.thinking_skill: one-to-one distribution to share fairly
j.notes: Major numerical contradiction: ten cookies become six with no explanation, which undermines the very counting lesson. Mama also appears without having been introduced as present.

j.learned_fact: A scab is like a lid that protects a healing cut; when it falls off on its own there is new pink skin underneath. True, though the scab falling off during one ball game is unrealistically fast.
j.thinking_skill: follows a rule and connects it to an observed result (scab off = new skin)
j.notes: Two themes (counting seats at a game, scab healing) sit side by side without connecting, and the scab conveniently falling off within one game strains plausibility. Sentences and vocabulary otherwise fit age 3 well.

j.learned_fact: A letter needs an address on it, or the mail carrier can't deliver it to the right house.
j.thinking_skill: notices a missing requirement and infers a problem
j.notes: Sequence glitch: she inspects the letter after it has already gone down the mail slot. For a 3-year-old the vocabulary (mail carrier, address, counter) and the line-waiting/ordinals detail push slightly past the band, though sentences are suitably short.

j.learned_fact: Rabbits' teeth never stop growing, so they chew tough plants to wear them down (true); rabbits eat grass and leaves, not cake.
j.thinking_skill: connects a cause to an effect (long teeth → chewing tough leaves)
j.notes: The five-senses labels ("That is his nose", "I hear him crunch with his ears", "I feel his fuzzy back") are bolted on and awkward, and Grandma's dental explanation is a mini-lecture; a few phrases ("wear them down", "twitched") sit above a 4-year-old's vocabulary.

j.learned_fact: Sound is vibration: a drum shakes when hit, and the eardrum shakes too — accurate, though a 3-year-old can't feel their eardrum vibrate, so the detail is fanciful.
j.thinking_skill: makes an analogy between two shaking things
j.notes: Three unrelated threads (swimming, drum/ear science, a bubble) never connect, and the eardrum-shaking observation is physically implausible. Sentences are short enough for age 3, but the science analogy and words like "wiggles of sound" aim older.

j.learned_fact: A triangle has three corners and a square has four corners (accurate).
j.thinking_skill: adjusts an action after a result (pours slower after spilling); sorts shapes by counting corners
j.notes: The shape-naming segment is bolted on to a breakfast scene, and the sudden stormy sky/rain at the end is a disconnected detail; "stormy" and "rain run down the wall" are odd for a three-year-old's vocabulary and imagery.

j.learned_fact: Cut onions make your eyes water even when you are not sad — true.
j.thinking_skill: tests a cause by removing it (onion near/far) and concludes
j.notes: A nurse carrying a pot of soup and an onion peel into a clinic line is contrived, and the "arm weak, ice cream will fix it" joke muddles the ending. For age 4 the sentences fit, but the inference chain and the counting-line setup are a bit advanced/busy.
